title: TU Wien Smart Factory — OT Attack & Operations
hook: Real factory-cell traffic: MQTT, OPC UA and Modbus/TCP, with attack and operational days. The Tuesday DoS day is unlabeled.
scenario: Captures from a real TU Wien smart-factory cell, mixing normal operational traffic with attack days. Industrial protocols — MQTT, OPC UA and Modbus/TCP — carry the process data. One day (Tuesday) is an unlabeled DoS: you have to characterize it yourself.
objectives: Inventory the OT assets and protocols.
Baseline normal MQTT/OPC-UA/Modbus behavior.
Characterize the unlabeled Tuesday DoS.
Distinguish attack traffic from normal process variation.

steps.title: Triage with Pcapper
steps.note: Pcapper auto-detects the OT protocols and runs the matching analyzers.

steps.title: Normalize every OT command with Pcapper

hints: These files are large (up to ~12 GB) — stay offline and use display filters, not the whole-file GUI.
Compare the unlabeled Tuesday capture's per-second rates against a known-normal day.
A Modbus or MQTT flood shows as a single source dominating the conversation table with tiny, rapid packets.
solution: No single answer — it's a characterization exercise. Baseline the normal days (MQTT topic cadence, OPC-UA sessions, Modbus function-code mix, per-second rates), then show how the Tuesday capture deviates (rate spike / flood source / abused function). The retained readme.txt labels the other days; Tuesday you argue from the evidence.
warning: OT capture is passive and safe to read. Never replay these onto a live industrial network.
credit: Brenner, B., Fabini, J., Offermanns, M., Semper, S. & Zseby, T. (2025), TU Wien — DOI 10.48436/ghdc6-45k78 — CC BY 4.0.

tshark.title: Inventory
tshark.cmd:
ls -lh data/tuwien-smart-factory/captures/
tshark -r data/tuwien-smart-factory/captures/s_day1.pcap.part000.pcap -q -z io,phs | grep -iE 'mqtt|opcua|modbus|tcp'
tshark.note: Read the retained readme.txt for what each file is.

tshark.title: Profile the protocols
tshark.cmd:
tshark -r <file>.pcap -Y 'mqtt' -T fields -e mqtt.topic | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
tshark -r <file>.pcap -Y 'modbus' -T fields -e modbus.func_code | sort | uniq -c
tshark.note: MQTT topics and Modbus function codes define the process baseline.

tshark.title: Baseline rates
tshark.cmd: tshark -r <normal>.pcap -q -z io,stat,1 | head -30
tshark.note: Establish packets/sec per protocol during normal operation.

tshark.title: Characterize the DoS
tshark.cmd:
tshark -r <tuesday>.pcap -q -z io,stat,1 | head
tshark -r <tuesday>.pcap -q -z conv,tcp | sort -k2 -rn | head
tshark.note: Look for a rate spike, a flood source, or a protocol abused to stall the cell.

title: Cyber4OT — Modbus Recon & PLC Hijacking
hook: 96 small Modbus/TCP traces: normal OT activity, reconnaissance, and PLC-hijacking / interruption attacks.
scenario: The Cyber4OT trace set: 96 PCAPNG captures of Modbus/TCP activity spanning normal operation, OT reconnaissance, and interruption / PLC-hijacking attacks. Small and focused — ideal for learning the Modbus attack surface precisely.
objectives: Separate normal Modbus polling from recon and attack traces.
Identify abusive function codes (writes to coils/registers).
Spot an unauthorized master hijacking the PLC.
Map findings to ATT&CK for ICS techniques.

steps.title: Triage with Pcapper
steps.note: Pcapper auto-detects the OT protocols and runs the matching analyzers.

steps.title: Inventory the traces
steps.cmd:
ls data/cyber4ot/data/traces/ | head
# read the accompanying README describing each trace

steps.title: Normalize every OT command with Pcapper

hints: Function codes 1-4 are reads (normal); 5/6/15/16 are writes (control).
A new source IP suddenly writing to coils/registers is the PLC hijack.
The README names each trace — use it to check your classification.
solution: Classify each trace by its Modbus function-code profile and source set: read-only polling = normal; sequential reads from a new host = reconnaissance; unexpected writes (fc 5/6/15/16) from an unauthorized master = interruption / PLC hijacking. The dataset README gives the ground-truth label per trace.
warning: Passive Modbus analysis only. Do not replay write commands toward any real PLC.
credit: Cabaj, K., Plamowski, S., Chaber, P., Ławryńczuk, M., Marusak, P., Nebeluk, R., Wojtulewicz, A. & Zarzycki, K. (2025) — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15005190 — CC BY-NC 4.0.

tshark.title: Triage the capture
tshark.note: Duration, endpoints and protocol mix before you dive in.
tshark.cmd:
capinfos 'data/cyber4ot/data/traces/Cyber4OT_001.pcapng'
tshark -r 'data/cyber4ot/data/traces/Cyber4OT_001.pcapng' -q -z io,phs | head -40

tshark.title: Inventory the traces
tshark.cmd:
ls data/cyber4ot/data/traces/ | head
# read the accompanying README describing each trace

tshark.title: Modbus function-code profile
tshark.cmd: for f in data/cyber4ot/data/traces/*.pcapng; do c=$(tshark -r "$f" -Y modbus -T fields -e modbus.func_code 2>/dev/null | sort -u | tr '\n' ','); echo "$c  $f"; done | head
tshark.note: Reads (fc 1-4) are normal polling; writes (fc 5/6/15/16) to a PLC are the interesting ones.

tshark.title: Find the recon
tshark.cmd: tshark -r <recon>.pcapng -Y 'modbus' -T fields -e ip.src -e modbus.func_code -e modbus.reference_num | head
tshark.note: Sequential register sweeps = enumeration of the PLC's memory map.

tshark.title: Catch the hijack
tshark.cmd: tshark -r <attack>.pcapng -Y 'modbus.func_code==5 || modbus.func_code==6 || modbus.func_code==16' -T fields -e ip.src -e modbus.func_code
tshark.note: An unexpected source issuing writes = the hijacking master.

title: 4SICS Geek Lounge — triage a live ICS lab (3 days)
hook: Three days of a conference ICS lab — real PLCs, RTUs and HMIs open to attendees. Inventory it, then catch the attendees misbehaving.
scenario:
At 4SICS (now CS3STHLM), the 'Geek Lounge' ICS lab — real PLCs, RTUs, HMIs/servers, industrial switches and firewalls — was open for hands-on testing by conference attendees, and Netresec captured the lab network for three days.

You are the lab's NSM analyst. Build an asset inventory from the traffic alone, learn what each controller normally does, and find the moments attendees did things a real plant would page someone at 3 a.m. for.
objectives: Inventory devices and vendors from protocol banners (ENIP ListIdentity, S7 SZL, LLDP/PROFINET DCP, Modbus device ID).
Identify each OT protocol's clients and servers.
Find scanning and discovery sweeps.
Find write, stop/start, download and other control operations and attribute them to a source.

steps.note: Writes, PLC stop/start, program transfer — attribute each to a source.

steps.title: Map it to ATT&CK for ICS
steps.note: Pcapper maps its detections to MITRE ATT&CK (Enterprise + ICS) and draws the attack path.

hints: Start from Pcapper --overview or tshark io,phs: the protocol hierarchy tells you which controllers were in the lab.
ENIP ListIdentity and S7 SZL (userdata function group 4) responses name the hardware.
Attendees scan first, then poke: find the scanner, then follow that IP's subsequent control traffic.
solution:
There is no single flag — this is open lab traffic. A good answer is an asset table (IP ↔ vendor/model ↔ protocol), the scanner IPs, and a timeline of the control operations (S7 stop/start or downloads, Modbus writes, CIP service calls) with their sources.

**Computed evidence (auto-extracted with tshark — verify it yourself):** S7comm operations — Read Var ×183070, Write Var ×68, Setup Communication ×16; dangerous-operation matches: 68 (top sources: 10.10.10.10 ×34, 10.10.10.30 ×23, 192.168.1.10 ×6); top conversations in 4SICS-GeekLounge-151020.pcap: 10.10.10.10↔10.10.10.20 (146,329 pkts), 10.10.10.10↔10.10.10.30 (62,611 pkts), 192.168.88.1↔192.168.88.61 (24,661 pkts) (basis: 3 of 3 capture file(s), first 300,000 packets each)

title: S4x15 ICS Village CTF — reconstruct the competition
hook: Captures from the S4x15 ICS Village Capture-the-Flag: PLCs, HMIs, BACnet and a corporate PC under attack by CTF teams.
scenario:
These captures were taken during the S4x15 Capture-the-Flag in Digital Bond's ICS Village — a mix of PLCs (Schneider Modicon, Allen-Bradley MicroLogix), GE iFIX HMI client/server, BACnet building controllers, an Advantech device and a Windows XP corporate host. CTF teams were scoring points by attacking them.

Reconstruct what the teams did: which devices were targeted, with which protocols, and what changed on the controllers.
objectives: Identify every device and its role from the per-host captures.
Find reconnaissance against each device.
Find the control/engineering operations that would have scored CTF points.
Build a timeline of the attacks.

steps.title: Overview with Pcapper (all hosts at once)
steps.note: Pcapper accepts a directory.

steps.title: Map it to ATT&CK for ICS
Let Pcapper hunt for the flag
steps.note: --ctf runs Pcapper's flag finder and decoders; --strings surfaces cleartext that a flag may hide in.

hints: The Modicon speaks Modbus (and Schneider's UMAS function 90); the MicroLogix speaks EtherNet/IP with PCCC encapsulated in CIP (service 0x4B).
The iFIX HMI captures show what the operators saw — and whether anyone else talked to the PLCs directly.
Look for BACnet writeProperty/reinitializeDevice against the building controllers.
solution:
Expect classic CTF tradecraft: discovery scans, then unauthenticated Modbus/UMAS writes against the Modicon, PCCC/CIP writes or mode changes against the MicroLogix, BACnet property writes against the building controllers, and IT-side attacks (SMB/HTTP) against the Windows XP and Advantech hosts. Score yourself on the device ↔ attack ↔ protocol table and the timeline. Netresec's S4x15 page links the original CTF description.

**Computed evidence (auto-extracted with tshark — verify it yourself):** BACnet operations — readProperty ×60048, readPropertyMultiple ×1897, atomicReadFile ×9; dangerous-operation matches: 0 for the BACnet filter (121,623 BACnet packets present, so the zero is real); top conversations in BACnet_FIU.pcap: 10.200.1.77↔131.94.238.11 (38,212 pkts), 10.200.1.202↔131.94.238.11 (36,656 pkts), 10.200.1.251↔131.94.238.11 (14,910 pkts); flag-like strings found by `strings`: none in plain text (decode protocol fields) (basis: 2 of 8 capture file(s), first 300,000 packets each)

title: Coimbra Modbus SCADA — MITM value tampering
hook: A man-in-the-middle rewrites Modbus values in flight. Prove it from the wire.
scenario:
The University of Coimbra built a Modbus/TCP SCADA testbed and captured clean operation plus a set of attacks for ICS intrusion-detection research (CRITIS 2018). Each challenge isolates one condition across the three capture sets.

A man-in-the-middle rewrites Modbus values in flight. Prove it from the wire.
objectives: Characterize the traffic in this condition.
Quantify the attack (rate, sources, targets) where present.
Determine the effect on the Modbus process traffic.
Write a detection for it.

steps.note: Three capture sets with several runs each — pick one to start, compare the rest later.

steps.title: Map it to ATT&CK for ICS

hints: Compare against the clean baseline challenge — the delta is the attack.
io,stat with per-protocol columns shows the attack and the process traffic side by side.
solution:
ARP-spoofing man-in-the-middle: the attacker's MAC appears for the PLC/HMI IPs and register values in the forwarded Modbus traffic are altered — compare values as sent by the master/PLC with what arrives after the attacker's hop. The dataset's folder/file names are the ground-truth labels.

hook: A Windows host on the SCADA LAN gets exploited with MS08-067 while the polling carries on. Find the exploit in the noise.
scenario:

A Windows host on the SCADA LAN gets exploited with MS08-067 while the polling carries on. Find the exploit in the noise.

title: TRITON/TRISIS — TriStation traffic of the SIS malware
hook: The engineering-protocol traffic of TRITON, the first malware built to attack a safety instrumented system (Schneider Triconex).
scenario:
TRITON (a.k.a. TRISIS / HatMan) targeted Schneider Electric Triconex safety controllers at a petrochemical plant in 2017 — malware designed to disable the system that keeps people alive. It talked to the controller using TriStation, Triconex's proprietary engineering protocol on UDP 1502.

Nozomi Networks Labs captured TriStation traffic of the malware's execution against a Triconex setup and released it with their tricotools. Analyze the protocol exchange.
objectives: Identify the engineering workstation and the safety controller.
Reconstruct the TriStation command sequence.
Identify the program/memory operations that correspond to TRITON's payload injection.
Describe how a defender could detect TriStation misuse.

steps.note: --safety detects Triconex/TriStation.

steps.title: Map it to ATT&CK for ICS

hints: Everything interesting is on UDP 1502.
Look for the program-download / memory-write style command codes and the payload-sized frames.
TRITON's known chain: connect, check controller state, append a program, then inject the payload into memory.
solution:
TRITON used TriStation to (1) identify and check the controller's state, (2) download a modified program, and (3) inject its payload (the inject.bin/imain.bin stages described in public analyses) into the controller's memory, attempting to persist a backdoor in the safety controller's firmware region. On the wire this appears as an engineering session from a workstation to the Triconex on UDP 1502 with program-download/write commands and payload-sized frames. Detection: any TriStation traffic outside a planned engineering window, or from a non-engineering host, is a critical alert — SIS engineering access should be physically keyed and rare.

hook: Someone tried to change a ControlLogix's clock and its Ethernet port configuration over EtherNet/IP. Reconstruct each attempt.
scenario:
Three captures of attempts against an Allen-Bradley ControlLogix (CL5000) over EtherNet/IP/CIP: changing the controller's date, its time, and its Ethernet port configuration. Clock changes break event timelines and scheduled logic; port reconfiguration can cut the controller off the network.

For each attempt, identify the CIP object/attribute targeted, the service used, and whether the controller accepted it (general status).

title: NIST robotics cell — baseline operation (CL001.1)
hook: What does baseline operation do to a live robotics work cell's control network?
scenario:
NIST's Cybersecurity for Smart Manufacturing Systems testbed includes a collaborative-robotics work cell: robots, a PLC and an HMI exchanging Modbus/TCP, captured at the cell switch and at each station. The captures are normal operation — no attacks — recorded while NIST exercised one low-baseline security control at a time.

This scenario (CL001.1) exercises **baseline operation**. Your job is the question OT defenders actually face: what does this security activity look like on the wire, and does it disturb the control loop?
objectives: Identify the robotics hosts (PLC, HMI, stations) and the security-tooling hosts.
Characterize the traffic baseline operation adds to the cell.
Measure the effect on Modbus/TCP polling (rate, gaps, retransmissions).
Compare with the baseline scenario (CL001.1) and decide whether this control is OT-safe.

steps.note: The cell-switch capture (capture.pcap) sees everything; station*/plc/hmi files are per-device views.

steps.title: Map it to ATT&CK for ICS
steps.note: Pcapper maps its detections to MITRE ATT&CK (Enterprise + ICS) and draws the attack path.

hints: capture.pcap is the switch view; per-device captures help attribute traffic to a host.
Scanners announce themselves: one source touching many ports/hosts in a short window.
A control is 'OT-safe' if the Modbus cycle keeps its rate and timing while it runs.
solution:
Normal operation plus baseline operation. Expect the security tooling's protocols (e.g. SMB/RPC for backups and AV, a burst of probes from the scanner for Nessus/Open-AudIT, syslog/LDAP/Kerberos for AD and logging) layered over steady Modbus/TCP polling; the analysis deliverable is the footprint of the control and whether the polling cycle degraded. NIST published these measurements to answer exactly that question.

**Computed evidence (auto-extracted with tshark — verify it yourself):** Modbus/TCP operations — Read Input Registers ×236532, Read Discrete Inputs ×235703, Read Holding Registers ×170356, Read Coils ×12544, Write Single Coil ×606, Write Single Register ×86; dangerous-operation matches: 692 (top sources: 192.168.0.30 ×346, 192.168.1.101 ×208, 192.168.1.3 ×51); top conversations in hmi.pcap: 192.168.0.30↔192.168.0.98 (54,685 pkts), 192.168.0.98↔192.168.1.104 (28,884 pkts), 192.168.0.98↔192.168.1.102 (28,803 pkts) (basis: 3 of 4 capture file(s), first 300,000 packets each, smallest files carrying Modbus/TCP chosen)

title: NIST process-control testbed — packet capture on a host
hook: A chemical-process control network (EtherNet/IP-CIP) during Wireshark capturing on a control-network host.
scenario:
NIST's process-control testbed runs a Tennessee-Eastman-style chemical process with PLCs and HMIs talking EtherNet/IP-CIP, plus DCE-RPC from the Windows side. NIST recorded one run per low-baseline security control; this run is Wireshark capturing on a control-network host. A process-simulation log (*_simlog.dat) sits next to the capture.

Characterize the control network, measure the footprint of this run's control on it, and decide whether the control is safe for the process.
objectives: Inventory the controllers, HMIs and servers.
Characterize the EtherNet/IP-CIP exchanges (implicit I/O vs. explicit messaging).
For the scan run: identify the scanner, what it probed, and any disturbance to CIP traffic.
Relate anomalies to the process log.

title: Industroyer2 — the real malware's IEC-104 traffic
hook: In April 2022 Sandworm aimed Industroyer2 at Ukrainian substations. This is its traffic.
scenario:
Industroyer2 is the IEC 60870-5-104 malware that Sandworm deployed against Ukrainian high-voltage substations in April 2022 — the successor to the 2016 CRASHOVERRIDE/Industroyer. Netresec ran the real sample in a sandbox against the three station addresses in its hard-coded configuration and published the captures.

Reconstruct exactly what the malware tells a substation RTU to do.
objectives: Identify the targeted stations (IP, common/ASDU address).
Reconstruct the IEC-104 session: STARTDT, interrogation, command sequence.
List the information object addresses (IOAs) it commands and the command types and values.
Write a detection for it.

title: Protocol deep-dive — DNP3 (221 unique captures)
hook: A deduplicated library of 221 DNP3 captures from 6 public collections. Learn the protocol's grammar, then hunt its dangerous operations.
scenario: Every public DNP3 sample in this range, deduplicated by SHA-256 across automayt-ics-pcap, cisa-icsnpp-test-traces, emreekin-ics-pcaps, inl-malcolm-ot-artifacts, iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps, suricata-verify-ics-tests. Use it to learn what the protocol looks like on the wire — roles, operations, normal cadence — and to practice spotting the operations attackers abuse: WRITE (2), SELECT/OPERATE (3/4), DIRECT_OPERATE (5/6), COLD/WARM_RESTART (13/14), INITIALIZE_DATA/APPL (15/16), START/STOP_APPL (17/18), DISABLE_UNSOLICITED (21), OPEN/DELETE_FILE (25/27), ACTIVATE_CONFIG (31).
objectives: Identify clients/masters and servers/outstations across the samples.
Enumerate the DNP3 operations present.
Flag every dangerous operation and its source.
Map findings to ATT&CK for ICS (T0855 Unauthorized Command Message · T0816 Device Restart/Shutdown · T0814 Denial of Service · T0856 Spoof Reporting Message).

solution:
A library, not a single puzzle: the deliverable is a per-capture table of roles and operations, with the dangerous ones flagged (WRITE (2), SELECT/OPERATE (3/4), DIRECT_OPERATE (5/6), COLD/WARM_RESTART (13/14), INITIALIZE_DATA/APPL (15/16), START/STOP_APPL (17/18), DISABLE_UNSOLICITED (21), OPEN/DELETE_FILE (25/27), ACTIVATE_CONFIG (31)). Sources are credited per collection in each folder's PROVENANCE.md.

tshark.title: Triage the capture
tshark.note: Duration, endpoints and protocol mix before you dive in.
tshark.cmd:
capinfos 'data/cisa-icsnpp-test-traces/icsnpp-dnp3/dnp3_example.pcap'
tshark -r 'data/cisa-icsnpp-test-traces/icsnpp-dnp3/dnp3_example.pcap' -q -z io,phs | head -40

tshark.title: Map the DNP3 conversation
tshark.note: Who polls whom? Masters/clients vs. outstations/servers, and the operation mix per pair.
tshark.cmd: tshark -r 'data/cisa-icsnpp-test-traces/icsnpp-dnp3/dnp3_example.pcap' -Y dnp3 -T fields -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e dnp3.src -e dnp3.dst -e dnp3.al.func | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -25

tshark.title: Hunt the dangerous operations
tshark.note: Flag WRITE (2), SELECT/OPERATE (3/4), DIRECT_OPERATE (5/6), COLD/WARM_RESTART (13/14), INITIALIZE_DATA/APPL (15/16), START/STOP_APPL (17/18), DISABLE_UNSOLICITED (21), OPEN/DELETE_FILE (25/27), ACTIVATE_CONFIG (31).
tshark.cmd: tshark -r 'data/cisa-icsnpp-test-traces/icsnpp-dnp3/dnp3_example.pcap' -Y 'dnp3.al.func in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 25, 27, 31}' -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e _ws.col.Info | head -40

tshark.title: Sweep the whole library
tshark.cmd: for f in 'data/cisa-icsnpp-test-traces/icsnpp-dnp3/dnp3_example.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_rec_time.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_file_write.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_read.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_file_read.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_link_only.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_del_measure.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_write.pcap' 'data/iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps/pcaps/bro/dnp3/dnp3_en_spon.pcap'; do echo "== $f"; tshark -r "$f" -Y 'dnp3.al.func in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 21, 25, 27, 31}' 2>/dev/null | head -3; done

title: Protocol deep-dive — BACnet (204 unique captures)
hook: A deduplicated library of 204 BACnet captures from 6 public collections. Learn the protocol's grammar, then hunt its dangerous operations.
scenario: Every public BACnet sample in this range, deduplicated by SHA-256 across automayt-ics-pcap, cisa-icsnpp-test-traces, emreekin-ics-pcaps, inl-malcolm-ot-artifacts, iti-ics-security-tools-pcaps, kargs-bacnet-captures. Use it to learn what the protocol looks like on the wire — roles, operations, normal cadence — and to practice spotting the operations attackers abuse: atomicWriteFile (7), createObject/deleteObject (10/11), writeProperty/writePropertyMultiple (15/16), deviceCommunicationControl (17 — silence a device) and reinitializeDevice (20); Who-Is (unconfirmed 8) is the discovery sweep.
objectives: Identify clients/masters and servers/outstations across the samples.
Enumerate the BACnet operations present.
Flag every dangerous operation and its source.
Map findings to ATT&CK for ICS (T0836 Modify Parameter · T0816 Device Restart/Shutdown · T0846 Remote System Discovery).

title: CSAW 2021 — The Magic Modbus
hook: CTF: The Magic Modbus (Modbus/TCP).
scenario:
A capture-the-flag challenge from CSAW CTF Quals 2021 — ICS. 

ICS CTF flags usually hide in protocol fields — register values, write payloads, function codes or timing — rather than in plain text. Work it like an analyst: map the protocol, find the operations that don't belong, then decode.
objectives: Identify the protocol(s), roles and endpoints.
Find the anomalous operations or payloads.
Extract and decode the flag.

steps.note: --ctf runs Pcapper's flag finder and decoders; --overview runs the right OT analyzer.

hints: Pcapper --ctf tries common encodings automatically.
Read writes, not just reads — the flag is often written.
Concatenate register values in order and decode the 16-bit words as ASCII.

A public write-up exists — work it yourself first, then compare: https://github.com/clevernyyyy/CSAW-CTF-2021-Quals/tree/main/ics/the_magic_modbus

**Computed evidence (auto-extracted with tshark — verify it yourself):** Modbus/TCP operations — Read Holding Registers ×228; dangerous-operation matches: 0 for the Modbus/TCP filter (228 Modbus/TCP packets present, so the zero is real); top conversations in modbus.pcap: 238.0.0.3↔238.0.0.4 (116 pkts), 238.0.0.5↔238.0.0.6 (68 pkts), 238.0.0.1↔238.0.0.2 (44 pkts); flag-like strings found by `strings`: none in plain text (decode protocol fields) (basis: 1 of 1 capture file(s), first 300,000 packets each)

tshark.title: Hunt the dangerous operations
tshark.note: Flag writes (FC 5/6/15/16/22/23), diagnostics (FC 8 — restart / force-listen-only), device identification (FC 43/14, recon) and Schneider UMAS (FC 90, engineering).

tshark.title: Decode the protocol fields
tshark.note: Register values, write payloads and odd function codes are the usual hiding places — try ASCII.

title: CIC Modbus 2023 — the substation's normal day
hook: Baseline a simulated substation: a SCADA HMI polling three IEDs over Modbus/TCP, captured per device and network-wide.
scenario:
The CIC Modbus 2023 dataset (Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity) simulates a substation whose SCADA HMI polls intelligent electronic devices over Modbus/TCP. Attack techniques include reconnaissance, query flooding, payload loading, delay response, length change, false-data injection, frame stacking, brute-force write and replay, launched from three vantage points.

Benign traffic only: the SCADA HMI and a central agent poll IEDs ied1a, ied1b and ied4c over Modbus/TCP. Learn each device's normal function codes, registers and cadence — the reference for the three attack challenges.
objectives: Identify the HMI, the IEDs and any attacker host.
Profile normal Modbus operations per device pair.
Find each malicious technique and its time window.
Write detections that work even when the attacker uses the master's address.

title: QUT DNP3 — Master flooding
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: a rogue master floods the outstation with DNP3 requests.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **Master flooding**: a rogue master floods the outstation with DNP3 requests. The dataset contains 36 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — Freeze-request flooding
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: a rogue master floods the outstation with counter-freeze requests.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **Freeze-request flooding**: a rogue master floods the outstation with counter-freeze requests. The dataset contains 25 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — Master session hijack + replay

objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — Outstation masquerading
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: the attacker impersonates the outstation toward the master.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **Outstation masquerading**: the attacker impersonates the outstation toward the master. The dataset contains 16 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — Outstation masquerading — spoofed counters
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: a fake outstation feeds the master forged counter values.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **Outstation masquerading — spoofed counters**: a fake outstation feeds the master forged counter values. The dataset contains 26 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — Injected warm restart
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: a WARM_RESTART (function code 14) is injected into the session.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **Injected warm restart**: a WARM_RESTART (function code 14) is injected into the session. The dataset contains 31 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

title: QUT DNP3 — MITM — inserting binary-input points
hook: DNP3 attack, one run, three vantage points: responses are rewritten in flight to add binary-input points that the outstation never reported.
scenario:
QUT built a DNP3 testbed — a master polling an outstation over DNP3/TCP — and used a Scapy-based attack framework to run each attack many times, capturing every run from three vantage points: the **master**, the **outstation** ("slave") and the **attacker**. Every packet of the master and outstation captures is labelled in the matching CSV (frame number, summary, label).

This challenge is one run of **MITM — inserting binary-input points**: responses are rewritten in flight to add binary-input points that the outstation never reported. The dataset contains 26 runs of this attack type in total — once you have solved this one, the others are practice.
objectives: Identify master, outstation and attacker (IP **and** MAC).
Find the attack window and every attack packet.
Explain what the attack does to the DNP3 session and the process data.
Write a detection that survives the other runs.

Labelled run of **MITM_modification_BinaryInputPointInsert**. The per-packet CSV labels are the exact answer key; the attacker capture shows the attacker's actions. Expected answer: attacker IP/MAC, window, the frames that implement the attack, and how they differ from normal master↔outstation traffic.

title: QUT S7comm — attacking the reactor
hook: Single S7comm writes that switch the reactor. Decode every one and build the plant's tag map.
scenario:
QUT built a small Siemens S7 process plant — a reactor, a conveyor belt with a diverter gate and a water tank, controlled by S7 PLCs and an HMI — and attacked it with crafted S7comm writes from an attacker host. Each attack run was captured from the **attacker**, the **HMI** and the **master** PLC.

This challenge contains one run of each attack on **the reactor**: ReactorOn, ReactorOff. Each run is tiny — the skill is decoding S7comm precisely.
objectives: For each run: which PLC, which memory area / DB, which byte.bit address, which value?
Build a tag map: address → process meaning.
Write a detection for unauthorised writes to those addresses.

title: QUT S7comm — flooding the process

scenario:
QUT built a small Siemens S7 process plant — a reactor, a conveyor belt with a diverter gate and a water tank, controlled by S7 PLCs and an HMI — and attacked it with crafted S7comm writes from an attacker host. Each attack run was captured from the **attacker**, the **HMI** and the **master** PLC.

These are the master-side captures of 9 flooding runs (ChangeUpperThreshold, ConveyorBeltGateChangeDirection, ConveyorBeltOff, ConveyorBeltOn, ReactorOff, ReactorOn, WaterTankOff, WaterTankOnAuto, WaterTankOnManu): the attacker repeats one process write at high rate.
objectives: Measure the rate of each flood.
Identify what each flood writes.
Assess the process impact vs a single write.
Write a rate-based detection.

tshark.note: Who polls whom? Masters/clients vs. outstations/servers, and the operation mix per pair.

tshark.title: Hunt the dangerous operations
tshark.note: Flag write variable (0x05), program download (0x1A–0x1C), program upload (0x1D–0x1F — logic theft), PI-service (0x28 — start/restart/compress), PLC STOP (0x29) and security/password userdata (function group 5); SZL reads (function group 4) are device recon.

title: ELEGANT — amplification DoS against multiple PLCs
hook: Amplification against several PLCs at once.
scenario:
The ELEGANT project (University of Coimbra) built a digital-twin testbed of Modbus/TCP programmable logic controllers and attacked it: denial-of-service (flooding and amplification, against one PLC or many) and man-in-the-middle (ARP poisoning, then the full attack chain). Each scenario was captured as rotating 10 MB files named cap_<n>_<timestamp>.

This challenge is **amplification DoS against multiple PLCs**. Quantify it against the normal-traffic challenge.
objectives: Identify the Modbus master, the PLCs and any attacker host (IP and MAC).
Find the attack, its start and its source.
Measure the impact on the Modbus exchange (latency, gaps, failed requests).
Write a detection that would fire on this scenario but not on normal traffic.

hints: The capture is a series of 10 MB files — mergecap them or work file by file.
Diff every number against the normal PLC traffic.
solution:
Labelled by the dataset as amplification DoS against multiple PLCs (folder multiple_amp_…). Expected answer: the attacker, the window, the mechanism and the measured effect on Modbus.

**Computed evidence (auto-extracted with tshark — verify it yourself):** Modbus/TCP operations — Read Holding Registers ×55809; dangerous-operation matches: 0 for the Modbus/TCP filter (55,809 Modbus/TCP packets present, so the zero is real); top conversations in cap_00265_20210314015502.pcapng: 192.168.10.2↔192.168.20.5 (13,965 pkts), 192.168.10.2↔192.168.20.4 (13,964 pkts), 192.168.10.2↔192.168.20.2 (13,961 pkts) (basis: 3 of 265 capture file(s), first 300,000 packets each, smallest files carrying Modbus/TCP chosen)
